steps.label: Introduction to Number Systems
steps.content:
Introduction to Number Systems

Why computers use binary, and converting confidently between binary and denary. Everything from yesterday, binary, denary, hex, binary addition and two's complement, is fair game all lesson.

steps.label: Place Value
steps.content:
Place Value

  • A computer only understands two states: on and off. We represent those two states as 1 and 0, which is binary.
  • Denary (base 10) uses columns worth 100, 10, 1. Binary (base 2) uses columns worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, each one double the last.
  • An 8-bit binary number can represent any denary value from 0 to 255.
  • To convert binary to denary: add up the place values of every column containing a 1.
  • To convert denary to binary: work left to right through the columns, taking away each column's value if it fits.

steps.label: Denary to Binary
steps.content:
Denary to Binary

  • Start at the 128 column and work right. At each column ask: does this value still fit in what's left?
  • If it fits, write 1 and subtract it from what's left. If it doesn't fit, write 0 and move on.
  • Every column gets a digit, even if it's 0. An 8-bit answer always has exactly 8 digits.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • Why does a computer only understand binary?
  • What denary value does the leftmost bit of an 8-bit number represent?
  • If I have 11110000, roughly how big is that number without working it out exactly? Is it closer to 0, 128 or 255?
  • When converting denary to binary, what do you write in a column that doesn't fit?
  • What's the biggest number you can make with 8 bits, and why?
